claims.claim: In anthropology, religion is studied as a cultural system: a shared system of beliefs and practices regarding the interaction of natural and supernatural phenomena (the OpenStax working definition).
Durkheim, in The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life, defined religion as a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things that unites adherents into a single moral community.

Geertz, in The Interpretation of Cultures, defined religion as a system of symbols that establishes powerful, pervasive, and long-lasting moods and motivations by formulating conceptions of a general order of existence.

No single definition of religion is universally accepted; Durkheim's empirical/structural definition and Geertz's symbolic/meaning-focused definition mark different poles, and anthropologists commonly cite both because religion spans social structures, beliefs, awe, and mystery.
Religious systems combine recurring elements: beliefs, practices (rituals), practitioners (full-time priests, prophets, and part-time shamans), and symbols.

Following Durkheim's functional account, religion supplies meaning (conceptions of the order of existence), builds community (uniting adherents into one moral community), and maintains order (establishing common value systems and forms of social control).

Tylor, in Primitive Culture (1871), identified animism — the attribution of souls or spiritual agency to things, including natural elements such as rocks and trees — as an evolutionary starting point for religion; the classification of religions by developmental stage fell out of favor by the 1940s.

Frazer, in The Golden Bough (1890), proposed a general development of modes of thought from magic to religion to science, analyzing sympathetic magic through the laws of similarity and contagion; the evolutionary sequence is no longer accepted.

Like all social institutions, religions evolve and adapt across time and cultures, responding to population change and to daily life; in state societies religion becomes institutionalized with full-time administrators, written doctrine, and recruitment by conversion.

The anthropological stance toward religion is descriptive, not evaluative: anthropologists describe and classify beliefs and practices as cultural phenomena without judging their truth, and terms such as animism function as classifications of practice, not evaluations.
Religion is a cultural universal: all cultures and societies across time have had beliefs and worldviews classifiable as religious in nature.

positions: Durkheim: a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, uniting adherents into a single moral community (empirical, structural).
Geertz: a system of symbols establishing powerful moods and motivations by formulating conceptions of a general order of existence (symbolic, meaning-focused).
OpenStax: a shared system of beliefs and practices regarding the interaction of natural and supernatural phenomena (broad working definition).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the broad working definition, attributes both classic formulations by name, and states plainly that no single definition is universally accepted, so readers see the debate rather than a false consensus.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Status of the nineteenth-century evolutionary schemes (Tylor's animism; Frazer's magic-religion-science)
positions: Tylor and Frazer treated religions and modes of thought as evolving from simpler to more complex forms, ranking societies in the process.
Twentieth-century anthropology abandoned ranking societies by developmental stage; by the 1940s the approach had fallen out of favor, and Britannica states Frazer's sequence is no longer accepted.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both schemes as intellectual history with attribution, explicitly notes that they are no longer accepted as explanations, and keeps only the surviving descriptive terms (animism, sympathetic magic).

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per this subject's source-map. openstax.org blocks direct fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture 20231030034347 of the canonical URL. Supports: the working definition (religion as a shared system of beliefs and practices regarding the interaction of natural and supernatural phenomena); Durkheim's definition (a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things uniting adherents into a single moral community) and Geertz's (a system of symbols establishing powerful, pervasive moods and motivations by formulating conceptions of a general order of existence); the statement that anthropologists bookend the subject with both definitions because religion spans varied constructs; the elements (beliefs, practices, social organization; specialists: full-time priests, prophets, part-time shamans; symbols via Geertz); religion's social functions (moral community, common value systems, social control); Tylor's animism as a proto-religion in Primitive Culture (1871); Frazer's The Golden Bough (1890) and sympathetic magic (laws of similarity and contagion); institutionalization of religion in state societies; and the statement that like all social institutions, religion evolves and adapts across time and cultures. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Do Mountains Have Souls? — SAPIENS (essay by Justine Quijada, published 2022-11-15)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per this subject's source-map (SAPIENS, anthropology explainer magazine). Read live 2026-08-22; the site notes SAPIENS has concluded publishing while its archive remains open. Written by an anthropologist of religion about the history of the term animism: the term was coined by Edward Burnett Tylor; it was originally used to classify religions and rank societies (animism to polytheism to monotheism); the classification-by-development approach had fallen out of favor by the 1940s; and animism is understood today descriptively as practices through which people cultivate relationships with beings in the world around them. Supports the historical treatment of animism and the descriptive, non-evaluative stance. No wording reproduced.
